I now have a complete picture of the codebase. Here is the structured review.

---

## Critical

**`/service/routes/users.py:16`** - SQL injection via f-string query construction

What: `user_id` is taken directly from `request.query` and interpolated into a SQL string with an f-string. Any value such as `' OR '1'='1` or `'; DROP TABLE users; --` will be executed verbatim by SQLite.

Why: This is a textbook SQL injection vulnerability. It allows an authenticated caller to read arbitrary rows, bypass the `id` filter entirely, or (in a write-capable schema) corrupt or destroy data.

Suggested direction: Replace the f-string with a parameterised query — pass `user_id` as the second argument to `_DB.execute` using the `?` placeholder (`"SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = ?"`, `(user_id,)`). The `is_valid_id` helper in `service/validator.py` already exists and should also be called before the query is attempted (see Important section below).

---

**`/service/routes/users.py:7`** - Module-level `sqlite3.connect` creates a single shared in-memory database at import time

What: `_DB` is a module-level singleton connection opened when the module is first imported. In any multi-threaded server context `sqlite3` connections are not thread-safe by default (`check_same_thread=True` is the default), so concurrent requests will raise `ProgrammingError`. Even in a single-threaded process, this couples every test run and every import to the same mutable global state.

Why: Silent data corruption or crashes under concurrent load; test isolation problems (mutations in one test bleed into another).

Suggested direction: Either pass `check_same_thread=False` and add a threading lock around all `_DB.execute` calls, or create the connection inside a request-scoped helper/dependency. Given the rest of the codebase is simple, a module-level lock guarding each execute is the minimal fix.

---

## Important

**`/service/routes/users.py:14-16`** - `is_valid_id` from `service/validator.py` is never called

What: `service/validator.py` was added in this same changeset and provides exactly the validation needed before the database query, but `get_user` never imports or calls it.

Why: The validator is dead code as shipped. Without it, `None` (when the `id` query parameter is absent) reaches the f-string and produces the literal SQL `WHERE id = 'None'`, which silently returns a 404 instead of a 400. Any other malformed input also passes through unchecked.

Suggested direction: Import `is_valid_id` in `users.py` and call it on `user_id` immediately after line 14; return a 400 response if it fails. This also handles the missing-parameter case cleanly.

---

**`/service/routes/users.py:14`** - Missing-parameter case produces a misleading 404 instead of a 400

What: If a caller sends a request with no `id` query parameter, `request.query.get("id")` returns `None`. The query runs (producing no row) and the handler returns `{"status": 404, ...}`. A missing required parameter should be a 400 Bad Request, not a 404.

Why: Incorrect status codes mislead callers and make client-side error handling unreliable.

Suggested direction: Check that `user_id` is not `None` (or falsy) before hitting the database and return a 400 in that branch. Calling `is_valid_id` as described above handles this automatically.

---

**`/tests/test_users.py`** - No test coverage for the missing-id, invalid-id, or not-found cases

What: The test file covers only "no auth" (401) and "happy path for known user" (200). There are no tests for: absent `id` parameter, an `id` that matches no row (404), or a malformed `id` value.

Why: The three untested branches include the exact input paths where the bugs above manifest. Once those bugs are fixed the new behaviour will have no regression coverage.

Suggested direction: Add tests for `qid=None` (expect 400 after the fix), `qid="999"` (expect 404), and at minimum one obviously invalid id like `qid="' OR '1'='1"` (expect 400 from the validator).

---

## Nice to have

**`/service/routes/users.py:7-9`** - Seed data mixed into route module

What: The `CREATE TABLE` and `INSERT` statements live at module scope inside the route file, coupling data initialisation to the HTTP handler module.

Why: This is not a bug, but it makes it harder to swap in a real database later and harder to reset state in tests without reimporting the module.

Suggested direction: Move database setup into a dedicated `service/db.py` module (matching the existing pattern of separating concerns into `service/auth.py`, `service/validator.py`). The route module would then import a `get_db()` accessor.

**`/tests/test_users.py:4`** - `_Req` stub is duplicated verbatim from `tests/test_status.py`

What: Both test files define an identical `_Req` helper class (modulo the `qid` parameter). The `test_users.py` version adds `query` support, but the base structure is copy-pasted.

Why: Minor duplication; not harmful yet, but will drift if the request interface grows.

Suggested direction: Move `_Req` (with both `headers` and `query` support) to a `tests/conftest.py` fixture so both test modules share one definition, consistent with standard pytest practice.
